An intention lock is never a substitute for the row lock it signals; it exists purely so a competing table-level request doesn't have to scan every row to find out whether it's safe.

Finer granularity (row locks) maximizes concurrency but multiplies the number of locks a transaction holds, which is exactly the cost lock escalation exists to cap; coarser granularity (table locks) does the opposite trade in both directions.

at.step: Predict: is finer granularity always better?

items.item: Detection and prevention solve the same problem from opposite directions: detection lets every transaction run and only intervenes once a real cycle has formed; prevention refuses to let a cycle-prone wait even start, using nothing but each transaction's own priority.

Wait-die and wound-wait never produce a real deadlock cycle at all, by construction — which is also their own cost: both abort transactions pessimistically, including some that would never actually have deadlocked.

Lock escalation's own trigger is per-statement and per-table-reference, not per-transaction: a statement touching two tables can escalate on one while staying fine-grained on the other, exactly as SQL Server's own documentation describes.

A long-running ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock is dangerous specifically because it is the one mode that blocks even a read; a lock that only blocked writes would be far less disruptive to a live, read-heavy production table.

Postgres's own deadlock_timeout default is a genuine engineering trade-off, not an arbitrary number: too short wastes CPU checking for cycles that rarely exist, too long leaves a real deadlock undetected and both transactions stalled for longer than necessary.

items.item: A deadlock caught by detection always costs one transaction a rollback and a retry; this is identical in shape to topic 13's own SSI false positives, even though the underlying mechanism (locking vs. snapshot conflict tracking) is completely different.

This topic's own consistent-lock-order experiment doesn't eliminate contention, only the deadlock: the waiting transaction in that reproduction still blocks for its own real duration, it simply never forms a cycle, which is the distinction a learner must hold onto to avoid thinking 'ordered locks mean no waiting.'

items.item: Neither SQL Server nor Db2 runs in this sandbox, so their own thresholds (the 5,000/1,250-lock figures, Db2's percentage-based maxlocks) are disclosed directly as sourced from each vendor's own current documentation rather than measured here, exactly as the chapter's own shared notation requires for a claim this sandbox can't run.

A migration tool that wraps a schema change in a short transaction and retries on lock-wait timeout is treating this topic's own ACCESS EXCLUSIVE hazard as a known, managed risk rather than hoping it never happens — exactly the operational posture the next topic's optimistic-vs-pessimistic framing generalizes.
